Two passes, one report

Some review items can be verified from outside by sending requests to your app. Others only show up in code. The tool does both and files every result under the review area it relates to.

Pass 1 · runtime

Probes your deployed app

Ordinary HTTP requests and TLS handshakes, sent from our scanner, your machine or your CI runner.

  • HTTP to HTTPS redirect, HSTS, trusted certificate
  • TLS 1.0 and 1.1 refused, TLS 1.2+ negotiated, cipher strength
  • Cache-Control: no-store on sensitive pages, not private
  • TRACE and TRACK disabled
  • Secure and HttpOnly on session cookies
  • OAuth callback answers with a 302, not an HTML page
  • Open redirects on common parameters like ?next=
  • Version banners and missing browser security headers

Pass 2 · source

Scans your codebase

Pattern-based scan of JS/TS, Python, Ruby, PHP, Java, C# and Go. It flags code to look at; it can’t prove code is safe.

  • Refresh token and realmId stored without AES or 3DES
  • Encryption keys or client secrets hardcoded in source
  • Tokens or authResponse passed to loggers
  • Tokens returned to the browser or put in localStorage
  • Constant OAuth state and missing state validation
  • CSRF middleware, disabled TLS verification, ECB and deprecated ciphers
  • SQL and QuickBooks-query string interpolation, XSS sinks, XXE
  • QuickBooks data code that also imports LLM, analytics or APM SDKs

Small mistakes that cost a review cycle

Most of these are one-line fixes. The hard part is knowing they matter before a reviewer points them out.

Copying the sample’s state value

A fixed state turns off CSRF protection on the connect flow. Generate one per request and compare it in the callback.

- authorizeUri({ scope, state: 'testState' })
+ req.session.state = randomBytes(32).toString('hex')
+ authorizeUri({ scope, state: req.session.state })

Using private as the cache header

private still lets the browser cache the page. Sensitive pages need no-store.

- Cache-Control: private, max-age=0
+ Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate

Rendering a page on the OAuth callback

The callback URL carries the auth code and realmId. If it renders HTML, third-party scripts or images on that page can receive them in the Referer header.

- res.send('<h1>Connected!</h1>')
+ res.redirect(302, '/app/connected')

Storing the refresh token as plain text

Encrypt the refresh token and realmId before writing them, and load the key from configuration, not from code.

- db.save({ refreshToken: token.refresh_token })
+ db.save({ refreshToken: encrypt(token.refresh_token) })
+ // key: process.env.TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY (AES-256-GCM)

What’s automated, and what isn’t

Some requirements are about policy and process, and no scanner can confirm them. Those go on a sign-off checklist at the end of every report. The requirements guide covers each item in depth.

Review areaCoverageWhat the tool looks at
Server & transportautomatedHTTPS, TLS versions, cache headers, HTTP methods, version banners, token logging in code
Cookies & sessionsautomatedSet-Cookie flags on probed responses; cookie settings in code
Token-endpoint redirectsautomatedHow your OAuth callback answers a test request
OAuth token managementheuristicEncryption near token storage, inline keys, tokens reaching the browser
Attack vulnerabilitiesheuristicOAuth state, CSRF middleware, open redirects, injection and XSS patterns. Pair it with a DAST scan.
QuickBooks data usagesign-offFlags third-party SDKs near QuickBooks data; the rest is your attestation

Run it on every deploy

The CLI and GitHub Action run the same checks, plus signed-in pages using a session cookie that never leaves your infrastructure.

npx quickbooks-review-check --url https://app.example.com --callback /oauth/callback --source .
1

Add the workflow

Drop the YAML into .github/workflows/.

2

Give it a session

Store a test-account cookie as a repository secret so it checks signed-in pages.

3

Read the job summary

Results and the sign-off checklist appear on every run. Choose whether warnings fail the build.

name: QuickBooks review check
on:
  deployment_status:
  schedule: [{ cron: '0 6 * * 1' }]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: apideck-libraries/quickbooks-review-check@v0
        with:
          url: https://app.example.com
          callback: /oauth/quickbooks/callback
          paths: |
            /dashboard
            /settings/quickbooks
          headers: |
            Cookie: ${{ secrets.QBRC_SESSION_COOKIE }}
          source: .
          fail-on: fail   # or warn | never

Questions

For the exact, current requirements, always go to Intuit’s own developer documentation. Found a bug or a missing check? Open an issue.

If everything passes, will my app be approved?

No. This is a self-check, not a certification, penetration test or security audit. It catches common mechanical issues. Intuit decides on approval through its own review process, which this tool doesn’t replicate and has no part in.

What happens to my code when I scan it here?

Nothing leaves your browser. The source scan runs in this tab using the same rules as the CLI. You can disconnect from the network after the page loads and it still works.

Why can’t I give the hosted scanner a session cookie?

Because we don’t want your session. To check signed-in pages, run the CLI or GitHub Action, where the cookie stays on your machine or in your CI secrets.

What does it cost?

Nothing. It’s MIT licensed and has no paid tier. Fork it, run it anywhere, and send pull requests for checks you want added.

Is this affiliated with Intuit?

No. It’s an independent open-source project by Apideck. Intuit hasn’t endorsed or reviewed it. Our summary of the requirements is our reading of Intuit’s public documentation and may lag behind changes.

What does the live scan send to my app?

About 30 ordinary requests: a few GETs, a TRACE, TRACK and OPTIONS, a test call to your OAuth callback with fake parameters, and redirect probes with a harmless test URL. Plus four TLS handshakes. Only scan apps you own or are authorized to test.

Why might it flag code that’s fine?

The source scan uses patterns, so it reports things to review, like an innerHTML that only ever renders static text. Treat warnings as prompts to look, and failures as likely problems to confirm.

Do I need to keep checking after approval?

Listed apps can be reviewed again later, so run the GitHub Action on deploys and on a schedule. A changed header or a new logging line then shows up in CI first.
